RESEARCH-LED IDENTITY EXPLORATION

A dwelling. A response. One identity.

A shared dwelling, made expressive through the response of praise. The containing space and the gesture of opening, gathering, or lifting should belong to the same form.

The name should be recognized before the explanation is known. The explanation should deepen a strong form, rather than rescue an arbitrary one.

Dwelling among a people

Exodus 25:8 links sanctuary with dwelling “among them.” Design for a relationship between sacred dwelling and people, rather than real estate alone.

Sources 1

Presence is more than an icon

Exodus 40 describes the cloud covering the Tent of Meeting and glory filling the tabernacle. Light, an opening, or a held interior would be contemporary artistic interpretations, not a graphic depiction of God.

Sources 2

Entering with thanksgiving

Psalm 100 connects gladness, singing, entering, thanksgiving, praise, and belonging. A threshold can explore invitation without pretending to reconstruct the wilderness sanctuary.

Sources 3

Praise extends beyond music

Psalm 150 names several instruments, dancing, and everything that has breath. The parish identity need not be led by any one instrument.

Sources 4

Context matters

Hebrews 9 describes earthly sanctuary arrangements and restricted priestly access, then develops its Christological argument. It is not a logo blueprint or a mandate for literal furniture.

Sources 5

Joined material, one dwelling

Exodus 26–27 and Numbers 4 describe joined textiles, covering, frames, screens, court, and transport. Coupling and a shared interior offer a fresh construction language. Historical reconstruction and archaeological claims remain outside the verified evidence.

Sources 6, 7

Exact public-domain WEB excerpts, mirror URLs, retrieval hashes, architectural limits, and typography licenses are retained in the browser study and research folder. Contemporary visual interpretations are not parish doctrine or archaeological reconstructions.

SIX TERRITORIES / MONOCHROME HYPOTHESES

Twelve investigated ideas / 01–06

01 / Responsive Cover

Joined textile folds make a dwelling whose own lifted edges express response and praise.

Advances because the covering and its upward response are the same draped construction. It offers the most direct dwelling association without a separate worship icon.

02 / Coupled Fabric

Separate textile lengths become one woven dwelling through a visible over-and-under relationship.

Set aside: the coupled lengths look like an industrial/technology monogram; the meaningful textile premise is better expressed by 01.

03 / Processional Court

A generous open perimeter brings entering and a common interior into one plan-like sign.

Set aside: its literal plan becomes a rigid venue/maze-like sign and the internal panels can look like a face. It is less welcoming than the brief requires.

04 / Returning Thanks

A continuous spatial gesture enters, gathers, and turns outward: thanksgiving as a response rather than a gate icon.

Set aside: the return reads as a P/e or wayfinding sign before it communicates thanksgiving. The explanation would carry too much of the idea.

05 / Held Light

A substantial surrounding form gives a white interior room to open upward, exploring presence through attention to space.

Set aside: the apparent flame or seed overwhelms the intended held interior. A white aperture must not be labeled as a depiction of God.

06 / Room in the Veil

The meeting of folded screens makes a luminous room rather than a façade; the unseen interior becomes the focal point.

Set aside: the hard portal and inner fragment feel like an architectural software icon. Its internal detail adds complexity without clearer meaning.

SIX TERRITORIES / MONOCHROME HYPOTHESES

Twelve investigated ideas / 07–12

07 / Common Ground

Unequal broad surfaces depend on one another to make a single generous room; gathering creates the dwelling.

Advances because interdependent surfaces visibly make one shared room; the generous opening gives belonging a spatial form rather than a ring of people.

08 / A Common Centre

Unequal organic contributions orient toward one generous shared interior rather than orbiting a leader or figure.

Set aside: the organic center reads too much like a generic community flower. Softness alone does not establish a parish identity.

09 / Cadenced Wall

A folded wall changes height and turns around a shared forecourt; the structure itself carries an expressive cadence.

Advances as a genuinely different, architectural way to test praise through cadence. Broad folded faces carry rhythm without instrument strings.

10 / Lifted Surface

A covering sweeps upward into one lifted fold, making shelter and expression arise from the same surface.

Set aside: the lifted covering overlaps the stronger dwelling premise in 01; the enclosing fold also risks a page/app icon.

11 / Shared Line

The first T becomes the common structure holding the full name together.

Advances as the strongest full-name alternative. The actual initial T provides the shared structure, making typography carry the identity.

12 / Lifted Praise

A steady dwelling-name is answered by a gently rising word of praise.

Set aside: the rising baseline risks campaign/event typography. The quieter, shared structural line in 11 offers a clearer long-term premise.

FOUR DEVELOPED DIRECTIONS / NOT AN APPROVAL

S1 / Responsive Cover

64px
32px
24px
16px

The main interior survives 24–32px. At 16px the finest tapered folds lose distinction; a separately reviewed micro cut would be required for critical tiny use.

The name, made visible

Tabernacle is the joined, sheltering textile. Praise is the lift and opening made by that same material. The form is a contemporary interpretation, not a reconstruction of the Exodus tent.

Construction

  • Four curved textile faces define one generous interior; the middle is a real open counter.
  • Diagonal breaks make folding and coupling visible; nothing is added inside as a second religious icon.
  • The silhouette is low and broad. No meaning is assigned to the number of pieces.

Typography

Source Serif 4 / 550 / optical size 24

The humanist serif supplies dignity and warmth beside the broad draped mass. Equal-sized name lines preserve the phrase; shaped kerning and deliberate spacing are retained. These are review outlines, not a final wordmark.

Open question

The white opening may suggest a robed figure or flame; the draped silhouette can suggest a tent venue or sails. Fine fold tips soften at micro sizes, and praise is less explicit than dwelling.

S2 / Common Ground

64px
32px
24px
16px

The shared interior and broad front opening remain visible at 16–32px. The secondary left crease closes at the smallest sizes, so it must not carry the core meaning.

The name, made visible

Distinct surfaces depend on each other to make one shared room. The gathering creates the dwelling; varied contours suggest collective participation rather than a single performer.

Construction

  • Four unequal broad surfaces surround one shared interior and a substantial front opening.
  • The surfaces rise and turn around the center; their relationship is the symbol rather than separate people or heads.
  • A fine overlap crease is secondary. The room and opening must remain recognizable when that crease closes small.

Typography

Instrument Sans / 550 / width 100

Open sans letterforms keep the full name welcoming and legible beside the more expressive spatial form. The calmer type lets the room carry the character; line lengths are accepted instead of stretching lowercase.

Open question

May read as an architectural/cultural institution rather than a church. The fine left crease closes small; do not assign doctrinal meaning to the number of surfaces.

S3 / Cadenced Wall

64px
32px
24px
16px

At 24–64px the fold sequence is visible. At 16px the articulation weakens into a segmented skyline; this is an unresolved limitation, not a passed favicon.

The name, made visible

A folded architectural wall gathers around an implied forecourt. Its changing heights and intervals make the dwelling itself expressive: praise as cadence, with no musical instrument.

Construction

  • Five broad filled faces turn through a measured sequence, keeping a visible relationship to folded construction.
  • Major seams are at least 12 units on the 256-unit canvas. There are no hairline strings or white overlays.
  • The lower edges hold an implied forecourt; changing height creates the cadence. Piece count is compositional.

Typography

Source Serif 4 / 550 / optical size 24

The serif counters the harder architectural edges with a human voice. The full name remains at the same type size and spacing logic as the other symbol tests, so the folded wall is judged on its own merits.

Open question

Could suggest a cultural venue, performance hall, or skyline. Rhythm is a creative association with praise; architecture alone cannot establish worship.

FOUR DEVELOPED DIRECTIONS / NOT AN APPROVAL

S4 / Shared Line

64px
32px
24px
16px

The compact T is tested separately at 64–16px. The complete wordmark is tested at 320/240px width; it is not claimed to be readable at 16px.

The name, made visible

The initial T becomes a common overhead structure and anchor for the complete name. “of Praise” inhabits that same typographic structure: the words carry the meaning without a separate icon.

Construction

  • A purpose-drawn initial T uses a 16-unit common beam, tapered ends, and a flared stem; Source Serif 4 weight 550 / optical size 24 provides the other letter outlines. Native kerning is retained. The horizontal arrangement uses the same grammar with a shorter stem; it does not stretch the text.
  • The two-line and true single-line compositions share a drawn initial and licensed Source Serif 4 outlines. The font binary is not modified.
  • The compact T is only a provisional derived initial; the full wordmark carries more recognition.

Typography

Source Serif 4 outlines + purpose-drawn initial T

The initial is constructed to hold the two readable name lines; other letters retain their licensed humanist shapes and actual kerning. The lighter developed beam gives the ascenders room. A single-line horizontal version uses the same grammar.

Open question

The long overhead line may read as a signboard or roof. The compact T has weaker distinctiveness without the full name. The single-line arrangement is very wide; minimum sizes and final clear space are not established.

RESEARCH-LED IDENTITY EXPLORATION

Four hypotheses for your review.

What advances

The four develop different kinds of identifier: a draped covering, a shared spatial enclosure, a broad architectural cadence, and a full-name wordmark. Selection favors a visible relationship to the name, silhouette distinction, and credible reproduction. The other eight remain visible with specific reasons. This is a development shortlist for your review, not a selection of the church’s identity.

Questions to answer

  • Which form feels like a whole parish rather than a building, choir, or venue?
  • Does the name-to-form connection deepen recognition without a long explanation?
  • Which alternative reading is acceptable, and which would undermine the identity?
  • Can the small-scale limitation be resolved without losing the central idea?

Decisions still open

Logo direction, final geometry, typography, palette, minimum sizes, material reproduction, and official RCCG pairing.

Evidence and limits

Primary scriptural wording was checked using identified public-domain WEB mirrors. Several scholarly sites were blocked; historical dating and archaeology are not independently verified. Research is a creative foundation, not an official parish theological statement.

The RCCG emblem remains a separate labeled reservation; authorized artwork has not been supplied. Typeface licenses are retained. Screen rendering does not establish physical reproduction or legal exclusivity.

No weekly flyer generator, final brand guide, or publication template has been created.
